topic: WorkOS FGA AI Agent Authorization Guide 2026

competitors.title: WorkOS FGA Documentation — Overview
key_points: FGA extends WorkOS RBAC with hierarchical, resource-scoped access control for complex B2B SaaS authorization needs
Core concepts: Subjects (users/groups/agents), Resources (business entities in hierarchy), Privileges (roles/permissions scoped to resource types)
Hierarchical permission inheritance: permissions flow down the resource tree automatically — one assignment grants access across entire sub-tree
Sub-50ms p95 access checks with strong consistency and high availability
Adoption path: keep RBAC for org-level, define resource types, register instances, introduce resource-scoped roles, add Authorization API checks
AuthKit integration: org-scoped roles in JWT for instant checks, resource-scoped via Authorization API

competitors.title: WorkOS FGA — Resource Types
key_points: Resource types define the schema of your authorization model — categories of entities and their parent-child relationships
Maximum depth of 5 levels, single parent per instance, up to 10 child types per resource type
AI agent platform hierarchy example: Organizations → Workspaces → AI agents, tools, datasets
Agents are both resources (users control who configures/launches them) and subjects (agents receive role assignments on tools/datasets)
Resource types managed exclusively through WorkOS Dashboard, not API — ensures intentional schema changes

competitors.title: WorkOS FGA — Roles and Permissions
key_points: Roles and permissions always scoped to specific resource types — workspace-admin applies only to workspaces
Permission inheritance: a workspace-admin role can include project:view, project:edit, app:view, app:deploy for child types
Permission naming convention: {resource_type}:{action} pattern (e.g., project:delete, workspace:edit)
Role naming convention: {resource-type}-{capability} pattern (e.g., workspace-admin, project-editor, project-viewer)
Custom resource-scoped roles per organization for unique access requirements
Scope and slugs are immutable after creation — use migration path for changes

competitors.title: WorkOS FGA — Role Assignments
key_points: Assignments connect an organization membership to a role on a specific resource — takes effect immediately
Direct assignment vs inherited access: role on parent resource with child-type permissions propagates down
Multiple resource-scoped roles always supported; multiple org-scoped roles require explicit enablement
Cascading events: resource deletion removes all assignments on it and children; membership removal removes all assignments
IdP role assignment for org-scoped roles (Okta/Azure AD groups) while resource-scoped roles managed via API

competitors.title: Delegated Access for AI Agents: The Intersection Rule Explained (WorkOS Blog, Jun 10, 2026)
key_points: The intersection rule: agent's effective authority = strict intersection of agent's configured permissions AND user's current permissions
Two access models: application-wide (service account, broad access) vs delegated (user's identity + scoped downstream token)
The ceiling problem: delegation alone isn't enough — agent's own role must cap what it can do even if user has sweeping permissions
Implementation: separate agent identity (OAuth client), pass user identity on every call, exchange tokens (RFC 8693), evaluate permissions in real time
Confused deputy defense: intersection rule limits blast radius of prompt injection — agent can't access what its role doesn't include
MCP authorization: every tool invocation should carry a token encoding what this agent, acting for this user, is permitted to do

competitors.title: The 2026 AI Agent Auth Checklist: 9 Things to Audit Before You Ship (WorkOS Blog, Jun 10, 2026)
key_points: Every agent needs its own identity (OAuth client with own client ID) — not shared service accounts or borrowed user sessions
Agent permissions = intersection of agent role and user permissions, never the union — runtime check per action
OpenID Connect for human auth, OAuth 2.1 for delegated authorization — separate purposes, separate tokens
Access tokens: short-lived (5-30 min), audience-bound (RFC 8707), scoped to task, with DPoP (RFC 9449) for high-security
Sensitive actions require explicit human approval (HITL pattern) — OAuth 2.1 auth code flow supports this natively
Tokens vaulted server-side, never in agent process or model context — credential gateway pattern
Immutable audit log with full execution context: user ID, agent ID, tenant, action, resource, timestamp, authorization context
Immediate revocation per agent and per user — short-lived tokens + server-side refresh token invalidation
Fail closed: authorization failures are definitive stops, not retries with different credentials

competitors.title: How to Manage API Keys, Tokens, and Secrets for AI Agents (WorkOS Blog, Jun 10, 2026)
key_points: Three-layer credential stack: Vault (encrypted storage), Pipes (OAuth connection management), Pipes MCP (session-scoped authorization)
29M hardcoded secrets found in public GitHub commits in 2025; AI-assisted commits leak at double the base rate
~24,000 secrets found in MCP configuration files on public GitHub — many following official documentation exactly
Gartner: by 2028, 90% of organizations sharing credentials with AI agents will need significant investment to undo this design
Principles: issue credentials per task not per agent, never let agents handle raw downstream credentials, segment by context
Session-scoped authorization: agent requests access, human approves session, agent invokes tools within session, session expires

competitors.title: AI Identity Is Your Next Security Blind Spot (WorkOS Blog, Jun 12, 2026)
key_points: Three patterns: service accounts for agents (static secret, broad scopes), OAuth client credentials for MCP tools, API keys for coding assistants
Inventory every non-human principal — most common finding is orphaned keys minted by ex-employees
Replace static secrets with short-lived credentials: OAuth client credentials with short TTLs or workload identity federation
Scope tokens to the job, not the user — 'read issues in this one repo' beats 'act as Alice'
Sync service identities through directory — treat agent identities as first-class directory entries, not side-channel YAML records
Log and alert on non-human principals separately — a spike that looks normal for a user is an incident for a service account

competitors.title: How to Secure Your MCP Server with OAuth Resource Indicators (WorkOS Blog, Jun 16, 2026)
key_points: Resource indicators (RFC 8707) bind tokens to specific resource servers via the `aud` claim — prevents token reuse across servers
Three risks addressed: token reuse across servers, confused deputy attacks, over-permissioned tokens
MCP auth flow: client discovers server metadata → initiates OAuth with `resource` parameter → receives audience-bound token → server validates `aud` claim
Implementation: advertise resource URI consistently, always validate `aud` claim, return informative 401 errors on mismatch
Clients need separate access tokens per MCP server, each with that server's resource URI
Resource indicators work alongside OAuth scopes — scopes define what actions, resource URI defines where
